TAX-DEFAULTED PROPERTY SALES AND THE TAX COLLECTOR'S DEED (REV. & TAX. CODE §§ 3691-3731, 4674-4675) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St, Springfield, CA · 063-0-190-045

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes what California law provides about the sale of tax-defaulted real property by a county tax collector and about the deed that such a sale produces. It is prepared for reference in connection with the property at 123 Main St, Springfield, CA, assessor's parcel number 063-0-190-045, in Ventura County, as to which Pat Morgan is identified as the person of interest. The sheet collects the provisions of Part 6 of Division 1 of the Revenue and Taxation Code that govern when the power of sale arises, what notice is required, when the right of redemption ends, what the tax collector's deed conveys and what it does not convey, how excess proceeds are claimed, and the time limits on challenging a completed sale, together with the published California decisions construing those provisions. It does not examine the assessment, tax, redemption or sale history of 123 Main St, Springfield, CA, does not state whether any sale, notice or deed complied with these statutes, does not value any interest, and does not recommend any course of action to any party.

WHEN THE TAX COLLECTOR'S POWER OF SALE ARISES: SECTIONS 3691 AND 3692
Chapter 7 of Part 6 of Division 1 of the Revenue and Taxation Code governs the sale of tax-defaulted property to private parties. Section 3691 fixes when the power to sell attaches: five years or more after the property has become tax defaulted, or three years or more in the case of nonresidential commercial property, the tax collector both has the power to sell and is directed to attempt a sale of property that has not been redeemed. The same subdivision states that any person may purchase at the sale regardless of a prior or existing lien on, claim to, or interest in the property. Section 3691 also defines "nonresidential commercial property" by exclusion, tolls the five-year period for property damaged in a declared disaster area whose damage has not been substantially repaired, and permits a county by ordinance or resolution to apply the five-year period to nonresidential commercial property. Section 3692 supplies the timetable for acting on that power and for reoffering property that draws no acceptable bid.

NOTICE TO PARTIES OF INTEREST AND PUBLISHED NOTICE: SECTIONS 3701 AND 3702
Section 3701 requires the tax collector, not less than 45 days nor more than 120 days before a proposed sale, to send notice by certified mail with return receipt requested to the last known mailing address of parties of interest as that term is defined in Section 4675, and prescribes what the notice must state, including the amount required to redeem, the fact that the property may be redeemed up to the close of business on the last business day before the sale, and information about the right to claim excess proceeds. The same section directs the tax collector to make a reasonable effort to obtain names and addresses, and then states the consequence of a failed effort: the validity of the sale is not affected if the reasonable effort does not disclose a party of interest or if a party of interest does not receive the mailed notice. Section 3702 adds published notice, once a week for three successive weeks, started not less than 21 days before the sale.

WHEN THE RIGHT OF REDEMPTION ENDS, AND WHEN IT REVIVES: SECTION 3707
Section 3707 fixes the moment at which the owner's statutory right to redeem tax-defaulted property is cut off: the right terminates at the close of business on the last business day prior to the commencement date of the tax sale. The section adds that the commencement of the sale is the actual sale date regardless of when the auction concludes, that a mailed remittance for redemption must be received in the tax collector's office before that deadline, and that the sale is complete when the tax collector has received full payment. Two provisions run the other way. Subdivision (d) states that the right of redemption revives if the property is not sold, and subdivision (a)(4) revives it on the next business day if a sale approved as a credit transaction is not paid for on time. Subdivision (e) states the consequence of the deadline passing without redemption for a person with title of record.

THE TAX COLLECTOR'S DEED AND ITS CONCLUSIVE-EVIDENCE EFFECT: SECTIONS 3708 AND 3711
Two short sections describe the instrument the sale produces. Section 3708 directs the tax collector, on receiving the full purchase price, to execute a deed to the purchaser without charge. Section 3711 then attaches an evidentiary consequence to that deed: except as against actual fraud, a deed duly acknowledged or proved is conclusive evidence of the regularity of all proceedings from the assessor's assessment through the execution of the deed. The rule is one of proof rather than of substantive title: it establishes the regularity of the steps in the tax sale process, and carries the express carve-out for actual fraud on its face. It stands alongside, and is qualified by, the limitations provisions in Sections 3725 and 3726 and the rescission procedure in Section 3731, each addressed in a later clause.

WHAT SECTION 3712 SAYS THE DEED CONVEYS
Section 3712 is the provision that gives a tax deed its distinctive effect. Its opening clause states that the deed conveys title to the purchaser free of all encumbrances of any kind existing before the sale, subject only to the list of exceptions that follows in subdivisions (a) through (h). The sale therefore operates differently from the conveyances documented elsewhere in this category: a grant deed passes whatever the grantor has, and a trustee's deed after a nonjudicial foreclosure passes title subject to interests senior to the deed of trust that was foreclosed. Under Section 3712 the starting point is the opposite, and the encumbrances that survive are those the Legislature has enumerated. The California Supreme Court in Quelimane Co. v. Stewart Title Guaranty Co. considered title insurance for property whose chain of title includes a tax deed; that decision is treated in this corpus's title insurance sheet and is not re-quoted here.

THE INTERESTS SECTION 3712 EXCEPTS FROM THE DEED
Subdivisions (a) through (h) of Section 3712 list what survives a tax sale. Subdivision (b) preserves the lien or other rights of a taxing agency that does not consent to the sale. Subdivision (d) preserves easements of any kind, including prescriptive easements, constituting servitudes upon or burdens to the property; water rights whose record title is held separately from title to the property; and restrictions of record. Subdivision (e) preserves unaccepted, recorded, irrevocable offers of dedication for a public purpose and recorded options of a taxing agency to purchase. Subdivision (g) preserves federal Internal Revenue Service liens that under federal law are not discharged by the sale even where the tax collector gave proper notice. Subdivisions (a), (c) and (f) address installments not yet payable, special assessments not included in the redemption amount, and unpaid assessments under the Improvement Bond Act of 1915, and subdivision (h) addresses unpaid Mello-Roos special taxes.

A RECORDED OIL AND GAS LEASE AS A "RESTRICTION OF RECORD": LEIPER V. GALLEGOS
In Leiper v. Gallegos the Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District, Division Six, considered whether a tax sale of property described in the deed as surface rights carried the subsurface oil and gas rights covered by a 1939 recorded oil and gas lease. The court read subdivision (d) of Section 3712 as excepting the recorded lease from the title the tax deed conveyed, on two independent grounds: the recorded lease is a restriction of record, and the interest it creates, a profit a prendre, is an easement within the subdivision's reference to easements of any kind. The opinion summarizes its own holding at the head of the opinion. It also relies on the principle, drawn from earlier authority it quotes, that a taxing agency which had no intent to assess a mineral estate does not assess it merely because the description on the assessment book is broad enough to cover it.

EXCESS PROCEEDS: SECTIONS 4674 AND 4675
When a tax sale produces more than the taxes, penalties and costs the sale must satisfy, the surplus is not retained by the purchaser and is not immediately retained by the county. Section 4674 directs that any excess remaining after the distributions required by Sections 4672 through 4673.1 be retained in the delinquent tax sale trust fund on account of, and subject to claim by, parties of interest as provided in Section 4675, and that unclaimed excess proceeds may afterwards be transferred to the county general fund. Section 4675 then supplies the claim procedure: a party of interest may file a claim with the county within one year following recordation of the tax collector's deed, claims are paid in a statutory order of priority that places lienholders of record ahead of persons with title of record, and an action to review the county's decision on a claim must be commenced within 90 days.

WHEN THE ONE-YEAR PERIOD BEGINS TO RUN: MAYER V. L&B REAL ESTATE
In Mayer v. L&B Real Estate the California Supreme Court addressed when the limitations period of Section 3725 starts against owners who remain in possession. Owners of commercial property learned after the fact that a portion of their parcel had been sold at a tax sale, and sued to quiet title. The court restated the long-standing rule that whether a limitations period bars a quiet title action may turn on whether the plaintiff is in undisturbed possession, and it identified the qualification on that rule: it does not apply once the owner has adequate notice that title has been transferred for nonpayment of taxes. expectedJSON.body: When a tax sale produces more than the taxes, penalties and costs the sale must satisfy, the surplus is not retained by the purchaser and is not immediately retained by the county. Section 4674 directs that any excess remaining after the distributions required by Sections 4672 through 4673.1 be retained in the delinquent tax sale trust fund on account of, and subject to claim by, parties of interest as provided in Section 4675, and that unclaimed excess proceeds may afterwards be transferred to the county general fund. Section 4675 then supplies the claim procedure: a party of interest may file a claim with the county within one year following recordation of the tax collector's deed, claims are paid in a statutory order of priority that places lienholders of record ahead of persons with title of record, and an action to review the county's decision on a claim must be commenced within 90 days.

expectedJSON.body: In Mayer v. L&B Real Estate the California Supreme Court addressed when the limitations period of Section 3725 starts against owners who remain in possession. Owners of commercial property learned after the fact that a portion of their parcel had been sold at a tax sale, and sued to quiet title. The court restated the long-standing rule that whether a limitations period bars a quiet title action may turn on whether the plaintiff is in undisturbed possession, and it identified the qualification on that rule: it does not apply once the owner has adequate notice that title has been transferred for nonpayment of taxes. Applying that framework, the court held that the period began only when the owners received the tax collector's letter telling them the property had been sold and naming them as owners, and that their suit filed within a year of that letter was timely.

citations.quote: It long has been the law that whether a statute of limitations bars an action to quiet title may turn on whether the plaintiff is in undisturbed possession of the land.

But the rule that the statute of limitations does not bar an action to quiet title by an owner in undisturbed possession of land does not apply if the owner has adequate notice that title to the property has been transferred for nonpayment of taxes.
Thus, the statute of limitations set forth in section 3725 began to run when the Mayers received the November 2, 2001 letter, and it expired one year later.
